tracks.title: Sharing shares contents
tracks.text: Lesson nine point five — sealed sections. A deep dive, under the VFS. Sharing shares contents. The bundles lesson ended on a warning… and this one picks it back up as a wound. When you share a bundle, you share its contents. Anyone you send the file to can unzip it. [curious] Which is exactly what you want when the point is to hand someone a working thing. And exactly what you don't want… the moment part of the disk shouldn't be readable. Picture three cases. First… a free demo carrying a paid dataset. Second… a shared dashboard whose numbers are public… but whose salary column isn't. Third… a client deliverable, where the result ships but the workings stay yours. The project should travel. One section of it shouldn't be legible. And here's the trap — every familiar answer is theater. A password field drawn over data the file already contains. A hidden sheet. An obfuscated blob. [sarcastic] They all assume the client will enforce the gate. But the attacker owns the client… and owns the bytes. Any check the client runs… the client can skip. A gate the client enforces is not a gate. It's a suggestion.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: So here's the definition. A sealed section is a region of a shipped disk that is encrypted ciphertext to everyone — whose content key never rides in the artifact. The key is escrowed at the runtime… released only after a posture check… and optionally wrapped to a recipient identity. Now, the envelope itself — the magic bytes, the nonce, the authentication tag, the fresh per-entry key — that was covered in the bundles lesson. This page is everything above the envelope. The binding that welds a key to its section. The release flow, with its real identity rules. What escrow actually is. And the wrap layer that removes the last honeypot. [curious] The envelope is the lock. This… is the locksmith.

tracks.title: A key welded to its section
tracks.text: A key welded to its section. Start with a subtle attack — because killing it explains the whole design. A sealed entry is just ciphertext with a tag. So what stops a holder from taking the ciphertext for the cheap section… relabelling it as the expensive one… and opening it with the expensive key the moment a broker hands that key out? Or a confused broker that simply returns the wrong key for the wrong section? The answer lives inside the authentication tag. When the engine seals an entry, it binds that entry's key id into the tag. Opening checks the same binding. So a key is welded to exactly one section's identity. Picture two hands reaching for two locks. The honest hand gives key A to entry A — the tag matches, and plaintext A falls out. The other hand — confused, or hostile — gives key A to entry B. The tag fails… because the key id baked into entry B is not A's. And the result is the same closed error — auth failed — not a wrong decrypt. [excited] And this isn't a claim. It's a cross-wiring test in the engine's suite — a broker that maliciously returns key A for entry B, asserting the failure. One more thing. The key id itself is no secret. It's mechanical — the prefix, then the path, base-sixty-four encoded. Seal the disk in a workbook named shop, and the key id reads shop, colon, d-m-zed-zed… and so on. The name of the lock is public. What stayed home… is the thirty-two bytes that open it.

tracks.title: The release
tracks.text: The release. If the key isn't in the file — where is it, and who decides you get it? The key is escrowed at the runtime. And one endpoint hands it out — a POST to slash, r-c-p, slash, key, slash, the key id. Same surface as any runtime call… with the auth plug running first. A sealed entry is gated by definition, so it enforces the strictest posture it has — gated data. And that demands a real, authenticated identity. Let me walk the request as one call with two endings. First… the opener posts the key id. Auth resolves an identity from a verified token. If there's no real identity behind it — null, an empty string, or the literal dev fallback user — the request dies at four-oh-one… with the same unauthorized envelope as any other rejected call. No oracle. A denied key release looks identical to a denied anything-else. Second ending… the identity is real. The gate enforces the gated-data posture, escrow is consulted, and an authorized caller gets two hundred — with the key id, the algorithm, and the key itself, base sixty-four, for a client-side decrypt. And a missing key, after auth, is an honest four-oh-four — because existence is only ever disclosed to someone already through the door. Read both transcripts plainly. With no credential — four-oh-one, error code unauthorized, and the body provably never contains the key. With a bearer token for a real user at a real org — two hundred, key id, algorithm, and a base-sixty-four key, thirty-two bytes. [curious] And the dev fallback — a tenant header, or the bare dev user — is refused on purpose. Only a verified token opens a sealed section. The whole path runs through the real router in the test suite.

tracks.title: The dead-man switch
tracks.text: The dead-man switch. Escrow is not a new database. It's the same lightweight, runtime-held state the host already keeps — an in-memory table on the running node. Three verbs live on it. First… put — it mints and stores a key when you seal. Second… get — it releases that key after the gate. And third… delete — which is revocation. Idempotent. One line. And that delete is the whole point. Keys are per section — so revoking one doesn't unlock the rest. Now picture one row feeding three mouths. Three shipped copies of a bundle — one you emailed, one on a USB stick, one a stranger forked — and every one of them dials the same escrow, for the same key id, to be fed its key after the check. Call delete on that key id… and the row is gone. So all three copies — wherever they are — become permanent noise… at the same instant. [excited] No key to retrieve. No decrypt to attempt. This is the real dead-man switch the envelope was built for. Not a remote wipe of files you no longer hold — the quieter, stronger thing. The files stay exactly where they are… and stop meaning anything.

tracks.title: Removing the honeypot
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — removing the honeypot. Skippable, if you like. An honest objection — so the runtime holds all the plaintext keys? On the release path so far… yes. Escrow stores raw content keys, and a breach of the broker would leak them. That's a honeypot. The wrap layer removes it. The trick is a sealed-box wrap. Generate an ephemeral key pair. Do a key exchange against the recipient's public key. The shared secret derives a key-encryption key… that wraps the content key. And now the runtime stores only wrapped keys — one per authorized recipient — never the plaintext. A breach now leaks ciphertext and wrapped keys. Still nothing readable. Reading takes two factors — holding the recipient private key… and the broker releasing your wrapped key after the posture check. Picture the wrapped-key envelope, the twin of the seal envelope, one layer up. First, five magic bytes — this is a wrapped key. Second, thirty-two bytes — the ephemeral public key. Third, the nonce. Fourth, the tag. And last… the wrapped content key. And the binding makes a wrapped key serve exactly one section. The key-encryption key folds in both public keys and the key id — which defends against key-reuse and unknown-key-share. So a key wrapped for one section cannot be repurposed for another. The info won't match… and unwrap fails closed. [excited] And that repurpose-fails property is a test, not a hope.

tracks.title: One identity, two curves
tracks.text: One identity… two curves. Another depth rung — the bridge math. Wrapping needs the recipient's encryption key. But a did-key identity is a signing key. Signing keys sign — they don't do key agreement. So does the recipient have to publish a second key, just to receive sealed sections? No. And not publishing one is the elegant part. The signing key and the agreement key are mathematically related. Follow two lanes. The top lane is public, and runs on the host. Take the did-key string. Base-fifty-eight decode it to the prefixed signing key. Recover the point. Apply the birational map — u equals one plus y, over one minus y, modulo two to the two-fifty-five, minus nineteen. And out comes the encryption public key… your wrap target. The bottom lane is private, and runs only on the recipient. Their seed, through a hash, then a clamp… yields the matching private key. [curious] So the host only ever needs the public map. The recipient keeps the seed. One identity, both curves, nothing new to publish. And it's pure field arithmetic — no native crypto library; the runtime carries only its standard crypto and a JSON encoder. Now the honesty note this lesson will not bury. The public map is not yet verified against published reference vectors. The candidate vector didn't match… and its provenance is unconfirmed. The round trip does pass — wrap, then unwrap, with the derived key pair. So the rule holds firm. The key-release endpoint stays escrow-only… until a reference confirms the map. The wrapped release is built, and adversarially tested, as a primitive — but it is deliberately not wired into the endpoint. Today, releasing returns the raw escrowed key to an approved caller. Full stop. We won't oversell a number the math hasn't been checked against.

tracks.title: The attack transcript
tracks.text: The attack transcript. The trust here is built by showing every illegitimate path… and its exact result. Each one is a test in the engine's adversarial suite, and every failure is the same shape on purpose — there is no oracle to probe, only a key you don't have. Let me give you the verdicts. Flip one byte of the nonce, the tag, or the ciphertext — auth failed. Strip the magic and feed the raw bytes — not sealed. Truncate the envelope — malformed… never a crash. A broker that returns entry A's key for entry B — auth failed, because the binding welds key to section. A wrong-size key from a buggy broker — an error tuple, not a crash. Unwrap with a different recipient's keys — unwrap failed. Reuse a wrapped key for another section — unwrap failed, the info doesn't match. A garbage ephemeral point in a crafted blob — unwrap failed, the raise is caught. And finally — a denied release, then an approved one. The sealed entry stays sealed… then opens to the identical bytes. [excited] That's the verdict of the whole table, in one line. Every illegitimate path lands on a closed, uniform error… and the one legitimate path — wait for the posture to approve — opens to the exact original bytes. There is nothing to learn from a failure… except that it failed.

tracks.title: Sealing the disk itself
tracks.text: Sealing the disk itself. Here's the tie back to the parent lesson. The sealable parts of a ship are the workbook's HTML shell… and the disk file. And sealing the disk seals the entire disk as one entry. Read the call aloud. Bundle dot ship — the workbook id, the HTML, the disk bytes — and then, gated, a list naming the disk file. Now what does the recipient see on unzip? The HTML opens fine — the shell is plaintext. The disk file begins with the seal magic, then a nonce, then a tag, then noise — and a database tool says, simply, not a database. And the manifest carries the only trace of the gate — a key-refs entry naming which entry, which key id, which algorithm. Never the key. The key id is just the prefix plus the encoded path — nothing about the name is secret. The secret is the thirty-two bytes that stayed home. And this is proven — the ship-sealed test asserts the HTML stays plaintext while the disk is a sealed envelope. One more thing. This composes with the privacy strip — a different wall entirely. The strip runs before sealing — unless you opt in, only the public workspace volume ships at all; memory and temp never leave. So… two walls, in one sentence. The strip protects what never ships. The seal protects what ships… locked.

tracks.title: Where the seal ends
tracks.text: Where the seal ends. The honesty section — and it's the real trust-builder, so none of it gets buried. First… granularity is the bundle entry, not a path inside the disk. Want one private folder, while the rest stays open? Today you seal the whole disk, or you restructure what ships. Second… escrow is in-memory. The keys live in runtime-held state on a running node. They do not survive a restart, and nothing re-escrows them automatically. Revocation-by-default is the upside — but durable escrow is your job today, not the system's. Third… the wrapped release is built and tested, but not wired. Release is escrow-only — the raw key to an approved caller — until the curve map is independently confirmed against reference vectors. Fourth… this is access control, not D-R-M. A recipient who legitimately decrypts can keep the plaintext. The seal decides whether you get the key — not what you do once you have it. And fifth… never bake a gated workbook into a public static file. Client-side gating is theater — which is exactly why the publish path carries an anti-leak guard. The publish step refuses to let a gate become a suggestion.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. Is this D-R-M? No — and that's the honest answer, not a dodge. It's access control. It decides whether you receive the key, after a check. Once a legitimate recipient decrypts, they hold the plaintext, and can keep it. What if the runtime disappears? Sealed sections go dark — the dead-man switch's other face. The key lives at the runtime, escrow is in-memory, so if the runtime is gone, the key is gone… and the ciphertext is permanent noise. [curious] Keep an unsealed copy of anything you can't afford to lose. Can I seal just one folder? Not today. The unit is the bundle entry, and the disk ships as one entry — seal it, and you've sealed the whole disk. Why can't I just put a password on it? Because a password gate is enforced by the client… and the key would have to ride inside the file for the client to check it. A sealed section's key never ships. Does the recipient need an account? For release, yes — a real authenticated identity. And what does the runtime see when it releases a key? On the live path… the raw key. That's exactly the honeypot the wrap layer removes — and until the wrap is wired, we'd rather you know that than assume otherwise.

tracks.title: Back up to the disk
tracks.text: So that's sealed sections. Not obfuscation. Not a forked format. Not a client-side guard — all bypassable, because the attacker owns the client and the bytes. Just a key… that never shipped. Escrowed at the runtime, released after a posture check, revocable in one line. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This deep dive sits under the VFS — the disk a section seals. And it starts right where the bundles lesson stopped — at the envelope. Read either one again… and the locksmith makes more sense.
